paper_title: Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Despite their extensive pretraining knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, large language models (LLMs) struggle to adaptively gather information in experimental design tasks. We study how to amortize sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) into an LLM by explicitly training the reasoning that guides action selection using information-gain rewards. Our approach specifies the experimental generative model independently of the LLM's own beliefs, allowing us to optimize expected information gain under a model of our choosing. We investigate the design choices for amortization, including alternative generative-model constructions, reward estimation, hypothesis-space specification, multi-step objectives, and computational costs relative to training- and inference-time BED baselines. On Twenty Questions, the resulting policies improve information acquisition and task performance, outperform inference- and training-time BED baselines at substantially lower computational cost, and generalize to unseen categories. We further demonstrate positive transfer from Twenty Questions training to Medi-Q, a real-world clinical dialogue benchmark. These results suggest that information gathering can be learned as a generalizable reasoning skill in LLMs.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Many real-world problems are not fully specified upfront, yet humans are remarkably effective at gathering the information needed to solve them (Li et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024). Consider clinician diagnosing patient. They draw on their medical knowledge to ask about relevant symptoms, think about possible diagnoses, and identify tests that can distinguish between them. As new evidence is acquired, they refine their hypotheses to decide what to investigate next. Effective information gathering thus requires both the prior knowledge to inform decision-making and the ability to continuously adapt those decisions in light of new evidence. Given their extensive pretraining knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored as agents in adaptive decision-making (Zhou et al., 2025a; Ashokkumar et al., 2026). Despite this potential, LLMs have been shown to perform poorly in multi-turn settings (Krishnamurthy et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2026; Laban et al., 2026). In particular, Gupta et al. (2025) demonstrate that LLMs are insensitive to experimental feedback, suggesting that their performance relies more on their (potentially inaccurate) prior knowledge than on their ability to adapt their reasoning to new evidence. In this work, we investigate how to improve LLMs ability to adaptively gather information. Rather than using an LLM to sample informative actions (Kobalczyk et al., 2025; Choudhury et al., 2025; Hartmann et al., 2026), we hypothesize that learning generalizable information gathering strategies requires explicitly training the reasoning process that guides action selection. We formalize this problem through sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) Rainforth et al. (2023), which uses generative model of the experiment to select actions that reduce uncertainty about an unknown quantity of interest. We investigate how to amortize this information-theoretic objective into an LLM reasoning policy using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Crucially, Authors contributed equally. 1 Preprint. training-time amortization allows us to specify the experimental generative model independently of the LLMs own beliefs. This means that we can evaluate actions based on their expected information gain under model of our choosing. We additionally investigate whether optimizing information gain over multiple interactions encourages non-myopic information-gathering strategies. We empirically show that amortizing BED into reasoning LLM develops strategies that generalize to previously unseen domains and tasks. Specifically, we train reasoning LLMs on Twenty Questions and demonstrate improved information acquisition across both seen and unseen categories. We show that models trained in this environment exhibit positive transfer to the real-world clinical dialogue benchmark Medi-Q (Li et al., 2024). Our results show that decoupling the experimental generative model from the LLMs beliefs improves information acquisition. We further find that rewarding expected information-gain rewards under our specified generative model improves learning relative to realized rewards, and that optimizing information acquisition over future interactions can improve sequential information gathering in non-myopic environments. Contributions. Our contributions are: We formulate amortized sequential BED for reasoning LLMs and study how to construct its generative model and information-gain reward (Sec. 4). We demonstrate that information-gathering behavior can be amortized into reasoning LLM, improving information acquisition and transferring across unseen domains and to different information-gathering task (Sec. 5). We systematically study the design of amortized BED, including alternative generativemodel constructions, reward estimation, hypothesis-space specification, multi-step objectives, and their computational cost relative to trainingand inference-time BED baselines (Sec. 5).

sections.title: 2 BACKGROUND & PROBLEM SETUP
sections.content: 2.1 BAYESIAN EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN Let θ denote an unknown variable that we wish to learn about. To gain information about θ, we can select an experimental design x, which results in an observation y. For example, in diagnostic setting, θ may represent patients underlying condition that we want to identify, diagnostic test, and the resulting test outcome. Because experiments may be subject to constraints such as cost or time, the chosen design should be as informative as possible. BED provides framework for quantifying how informative potential design is using generative model of the experiment, p(θ, x) = p(θ)p(y θ, x). Here, the prior p(θ) represents our initial beliefs about θ and the likelihood p(y θ, x) describes the probability of observing given θ and x. After selecting and observing y, these beliefs are updated through the posterior p(θ y, x). The informativeness of potential design is then quantified by its expected information gain (EIG): EIG(x) = Ep(θ)p(yθ,x) [log p(θ y, x) log p(θ)] = Ep(θ)p(yθ,x) [log p(y θ, x) log p(y x)] , (1) (2) which measures how much information design will provide about θ, in expectation over possible θ and observations y. Using Bayes rule, the EIG can be seen as either the expected reduction in uncertainty about θ after observing (Eq. 1) or the expected reduction in uncertainty about from knowing θ (Eq. 2). The optimal one-step design is defined as = arg maxxX EIG(x), where denotes the space of designs. This formulation extends naturally to the sequential setting where the design at step is chosen based on the history of previous experiments, ht1 = (x1, y1, . . . , xt1, yt1) by maximizing the EIG under the updated belief p(θ ht1). The experimental design at step can then be selected as = arg maxxX EIG(x; ht1). Challenges of Design Selection. Selecting designs according to the EIG in adaptive settings presents two major challenges. First, optimizing the EIG requires costly estimation of the posterior p(θ 2 Preprint. x1:t, y1:t) at each step, which depends on the observed interaction history and therefore cannot be computed in advance. Moreover, even given this posterior, calculating the EIG is doubly intractable: it involves an outer expectation over possible latent states and observations, and an inner marginalization over latent states to compute the posterior predictive distribution p(yt xt, ht1). Repeating this estimation and optimization procedure after every observation can be prohibitively expensive for settings that require decisions to be made in real time. Second, one-step EIG optimization considers only the immediate next design. This can be suboptimal in non-myopic decision states, where acquiring more information in the future requires first selecting design with limited immediate information gain.

sections.title: 2.2 AMORTIZING SEQUENTIAL EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN
sections.content: To address the computational cost of optimizing the EIG at inference time, Deep Adaptive Design (DAD, Foster et al. (2021)) amortizes sequential experimental design into design policy πϕ(xt ht1), which maps the history ht1 to the next design xt. This shifts the computational cost to training, allowing the learned policy to directly select the next design at inference time without EIG optimization. Under this design-policy perspective, the standard sequential BED procedure described above corresponds to an implicit policy πS, which selects each design by updating the posterior and optimizing the one-step EIG (Foster et al., 2021). Amortizing this policy directly would therefore require repeatedly simulating this expensive sequential BED procedure to generate training targets. Instead, DAD observes that the total EIG of sequential experiment is equal to the sum of its conditional EIGs across steps. Summing these conditional information gains gives the information gained between the initial prior and the posterior after the complete trajectory. Applying Bayes rule then expresses this quantity directly in terms of trajectory likelihoods: IT (π) = Ep(θ)p(hT θ,π) [log p(hT θ, π) log p(hT π)] , where p(hT π) = Ep(θ) [p(hT θ, π)] . sections.title: 4 METHOD: AMORTIZING BED IN REASONING LLMS
sections.content: Our goal is to amortize sequential BED into reasoning LLM. One approach to using an LLM as policy is to directly sample design given an interaction history, πϕ(xt ht1), and optimize its expected information gain (Hartmann et al., 2026). Instead, our aim is to train an LLM that can reason through limited information: deliberating over which hypotheses remain plausible, how possible observations distinguish them, and which further experiments those observations may enable. We therefore parameterize the policy as πϕ(zt, xt ht1) = πϕ(zt ht1) πϕ(xt ht1, zt). and train its joint output (zt, xt) with an information gain objective. At high level, our training procedure consists of three steps: (5) 1. Generate design through reasoning. Given an interaction history ht1, the policy generates reasoning trace zt followed by design xt. 2. Evaluate its information value. generative model, specified independently of the policy, provides the hypothesis and outcome distributions used to compute the information gain of the design xt. 3. Optimize the reasoning policy. We use information-gain rewards accumulated over K-step rollouts to train the reasoning policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024). This procedure requires two main design choices: how to construct the generative model used to evaluate information gain (Sec. 4.1), and how to turn this information signal into training reward (Sec. 4.2). 4.1 HOW SHOULD THE GENERATIVE MODEL p(θ, y; x) BE CONSTRUCTED? Estimating the EIG requires specifying generative model p(θ, y; x) of the experiment. In our amortized setting, this choice determines both the quality of the training signal and the computational cost of obtaining it. We build on the contrastive formulation in Sec. 2.2, which requires specifying two components: prior p(θ) over contrastive hypotheses and likelihood p(y θ, x) for evaluating proposed designs. We describe how we construct these components below. 4 Preprint. Decoupling the generative model from the policy. One option is to use the policy LLM itself to estimate both components, as in the approaches discussed in Sec. 3. Training-time amortization enables an important flexibility: the generative model can instead be specified independently of the policy being trained, without requiring it for design selection at inference time. This allows us to define the experimental distribution used for training upfront, while keeping it fixed as the policy is updated (see Appendix D.6). This is particularly useful when the initial policy provides poor approximation of that distribution. For example, the training prior can place mass on hypotheses that the policy itself would be unlikely to generate, while separate likelihood model can provide more reliable estimates of p(y θ, x) than the policys own predictive distribution. The prior p(θ). The contrastive hypotheses can be sampled from the prior for each trajectory, as in sPCE, or fixed across training. We define our prior as uniform distribution over finite contrastive set ΘC = {θℓ}L ℓ=0, with pC(θℓ) = 1/(L + 1). This prior is fixed across all training trajectories and defines the hypothesis distribution with respect to which information gain is computed. The size of the set introduces trade-off between coverage and computational cost, while its composition and prior weights determine which hypotheses the policy is trained to distinguish. The likelihood p(y θ, x). In an open-ended natural-language design space, the possible designs cannot generally be enumerated in advance, making it impractical to precompute their likelihoods. We therefore use separate, larger LLM as semantic likelihood evaluator poracle(y θ, x), which can be queried during training. Following Blau et al. (2022), we assume that each observation is conditionally independent of the interaction history given the hypothesis and current design, allowing us to accumulate likelihoods as Ct,ℓ (see Sec. 2.2). The observation may be stochastic even when θ is known. For example, the answer to Is it cute? is ambiguous for fixed θ (Choudhury et al., 2025). We therefore retain the full likelihood distribution over the finite outcome space Y. Each possible outcome induces corresponding updated likelihood, (y) t,ℓ = Ct1,ℓporacle(y θℓ, xt), which allows us to marginalize over possible outcomes when computing the reward (discussed in Sec. 4.2). This design also allows for likelihood evaluations poracle(y θℓ, xt) to be cached and reused across training. 4.2 HOW SHOULD THE REWARD BE ASSIGNED? sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We now evaluate our approach for amortizing sequential BED in reasoning LLM in four studies: Section Question 5.1 5.2 5.3 5.4 Does amortizing BED into reasoning LLM improve general information acquisition? How does our approach compare to existing inferenceand training-time BED approaches? How do choices for estimating and optimizing information gain affect performance? Does policy trained for information acquisition in one task transfer to different task? Training Environment Following prior work (Kobalczyk et al., 2025; Choudhury et al., 2025; Hartmann et al., 2026), we use Twenty Questions (TQ), where an agent must identify hidden target within 20 questions. Here, θ is the target (e.g., horse), is an open-ended natural-language question (e.g., Is it mammal?), and the observation lies in the finite answer space = {yes, no, maybe}. We use GPT-5 as the semantic likelihood evaluator p(yθ, x). Training Data Our main experiments train on the Animals domain. We use fixed contrastive set of 200 animals for computing the training reward, of which 100 are used as ground-truth targets θ when constructing training trajectories. We use GPT-5 to generate 250 Twenty Questions games over these 100 targets. From each game, we sample up to five intermediate points before the final guess, yielding 1,200 partial trajectories. Each sampled trajectory defines history ht1 containing the sequence of questions and answers observed up to that point. The task-transfer experiment uses separate training dataset, described in Sec. 5.4. Evaluation Data. Each model plays 50 Twenty Questions games across three seeds, with different target sampled for each game in the corresponding evaluation domain. We evaluate on held-out animals drawn from the same 200-animal contrastive set used during training. In Sec. 5.3, we consider animals that are absent from both the training targets and the training contrastive set. To assess cross-domain transfer, we evaluate on Plants, Celebrities, and Countries. Sec. 5.4 evaluates task transfer by applying models trained on Twenty Questions to MEDIQ (Li et al., 2024), an interactive medical question-asking benchmark. Models and Hyperparameters We call our method Amortized Reasoning for Bayesian Experimental Design (AR-BED). Unless otherwise specified, AR-BEDK is Gemma-4-E4B-it reasoning policy trained with expected information rewards with rollout horizon K. We denote by AR-BEDDirect the ablation where we train without reasoning, directly sampling and rewarding question from the history p(.h). We use batch size of 128 with 8 rollouts per state, and train for 250 steps. For multi-step training (K > 1), we set γ = 0.5. Full training details are in Appendix C. Metrics. We report the solve rate within 20-question budget and the average EIG per turn to account for varying game lengths. 6 Preprint. sections.title: 5.1 AMORTIZING BED INTO REASONING IMPROVES GENERAL INFORMATION ACQUISITION
sections.content: Setup. We evaluate whether amortizing BED into the reasoning process improves information acquisition both inand out-of-distribution. We compare our model, AR-BED1, to four controls: the BASE model and the directly trained AR-BEDDirect model, each evaluated with and without reasoning at inference time. This design separates gains from BED training from gains due only to enabling reasoning at test time. 1 Results.  (Fig. 1)  Adding reasoning to the BASE model reduces final solve rate across all categories and increases average EIG only on Countries. This suggests that inference-time reasoning alone does not improve information gathering, and may even worsen it.1 Training non-reasoning policy improves the in-distribution behavior but the transfer to out-of-distribution domains is inconsistent: it is worse than BASE on Plants but improves on Celebrities and Countries. This suggests that direct amortization can learn useful in-distribution question-sampling behavior, but does not produce robust transfer across domains. In contrast, our model AR-BED1 achieves the best final solve rate across all categories and obtains the highest average EIG per turn on Animals, Plants, and Countries. These gains over both the BASE model and the direct policy suggest that training reasoning model may enable general information-gathering strategies. 5.2 AMORTIZING BED INTO REASONING OUTPERFORMS INFERENCEAND TRAINING-TIME BED BASELINES Setup. We next compare against BED-style alternatives that differ in how they obtain the generative model used to estimate EIG. Our AR-BED1 model uses an external generative model, whereas BED-LLM (Choudhury et al., 2025) uses the LLM itself to construct the predictive generative model at inference time. We also compare to ASIG, training-time amortization baseline, which uses the same BED-LLM-style LLM-generated model during training but trains direct question-sampling policy rather than reasoning policy (Hartmann et al., 2026). To isolate the effect of the informationgain objective, we do not include an additional game reward for ASIG. We evaluate ASIG with and without reasoning at inference. Model Setting Results. Figure 3 shows that AR-BED1 outperforms the inference-time and training-time BED baselines on most domains. BED-LLM improves only modestly over the reasoning BASE model, and is worse than the non-reasoning BASE model on some domains in both solve rate and EIG. This suggests that online BED with an LLM-generated model of the experiment may be limited by the models ability to represent the relevant distributions p(θ) and p(y θ, x). Similarly, ASIG without reasoning does not improve over the non-reasoning BASE model, indicating that directly amortizing this LLM-generated BED objective suffers from similar limitations. Adding reasoning at inference substantially improves ASIG, but it still remains below AR-BED1 on Animals, Plants, and Countries, and is comparable on Celebrities. Both models are prompted to guess in the category Animals. As result, the mammals-trained model received flawed information signal compared to the true hypothesis space p(θ): for example, the question Is it mammal? receives EIG 0 despite being strong question to discriminate between animals. Fig. 2 shows the solve rate of both models on held-out sets of 25 mammals and 25 non-mammals. Notably, it also leads to worse performance than the animals-trained model on mammal targets. This suggests that training on the broader hypothesis space of animals might provide exposure to diversity of features that is beneficial even within the shared mammal subset. sections.title: 5.3.3 USING A NON-MYOPIC REWARD SIGNAL
sections.content: Appendix B.3 brings together three complementary evaluations of multi-step rewards. In naturallanguage adaptation of Cube-NM (Schütz et al., 2026), the two-step policy learns to acquire initially uninformative context for its downstream benefit, substantially outperforming the one-step policy in later disease identification. On the TwentyQuestions target-prediction task of Wang et al. (2025), multi-step policies improve attribute prediction, particularly on medium and hard questions. Finally, we empirically investigate the extent to which Twenty Questions as played by the GPT-5 policy shows signs of non-myopicity. We show that immediateand downstream-EIG rankings can differ, while matched-state evaluations find some gains from = 2 and = 3 over = 1 at twoand three-question horizons. Together, these results distinguish controlled non-myopic mechanism from the smaller benefits of lookahead in open-ended questioning. 5.4 GENERALIZATION TO OTHER TASKS The preceding experiments examine transfer across domains within TQ. We now ask whether the learned information-gathering behavior also transfers to different task. We use MediQ (Li et al., 2024), which simulates clinical questioning: given partial patient information and multiple-choice medical inquiry, policy asks open-ended questions to gather evidence from an LLM-based Patient with full access to patient records. Setup. We construct three synthetic medical TQ environments dermatology, neurology, and gastroenterologyeach with 50-disease contrastive set drawn from MediQs answer inventory. Using the AR-BED1 objective, we train separate medical policy on 1,200 starting states and evaluate its checkpoint against the base model. Both policies ask five questions with GPT-5 as the fixed Patient. We evaluate the quality of each models line of questioning by using separate GPT-5 decider to predict the answer from the initial information and interaction history. We report two diagnosis subsets: 95 dermatology cases whose correct diagnoses are absent from the training contrastive set (same domain, different task, held-out labels), and 92 cases from other specialties, including pediatrics, psychiatry, and cardiology (different domain and task). Full training and evaluation details are in Appendix C.4. Results. Table 3 shows that medical AR-BED1 improves accuracy from 90.5% to 94.7% on held-out dermatology diagnoses and from 84.8% to 90.2% on other specialties. It also increases the probability assigned to the correct answer and reduces the Brier score in both domains. These results indicate that the reasoning capabilities learned by AR-BED1 in synthetic TQ environment transfer to realistic, simulated clinical dialogue setting, including medical specialties not used during fine-tuning.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We studied how sequential Bayesian experimental design can be amortized into reasoning LLM to improve adaptive information gathering. Our approach makes two key design choices: decoupling the experimental generative model from the policy to avoid relying on potentially poor predictive distributions, and constructing expected information-gain rewards that can be accumulated across interactions. We find that our method improves information acquisition across unseen hypothesis spaces, outperforming other methods, and that the learned behavior transfers to Medi-Q, real-world 9 Preprint. clinical dialogue dataset. Our results suggest that adaptive information gathering can be learned as transferable reasoning capability in LLMs rather than reconstructed through explicit search at every interaction. Limitations. We study relatively short rollout horizons. Extending the approach to longer horizons while maintaining reliable training signal is an important direction. We also find that performance is sensitive to the coverage of the contrastive hypothesis set when it is misspecified relative to the true hypothesis space. Further understanding how the size, composition, and prior weighting of the contrastive set affect learning and transfer is therefore an important avenue for future study.

sections.title: A EXTENDED RELATED WORKS
sections.content: Inference-time BED. Methods for task disambiguation and adaptive questioning use LLM-generated hypotheses and response predictions to select questions by estimated EIG (Kobalczyk et al., 2025; Choudhury et al., 2025); related agents maintain explicit Bayesian beliefs to guide exploration (Grand et al., 2026). These approaches require repeated belief maintenance and utility evaluation at deployment. While one-step EIG selection is myopic, uncertainty-aware planning and conversation-tree search incorporate simulated future interactions (Hu et al., 2024; Arnould et al., 2026). Thus, nonmyopic information gathering is not unique to trained policies; our aim is to amortize this behavior into reasoning LLM rather than perform explicit design search at inference time. Training-time BED. Information-driven post-training uses EIG-ranked question preferences (Mazzaccara et al., 2024) or dense rewards based on changes in the models confidence in known target (Auzina et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2026). These approaches establish informative questioning as learnable behavior, but differ in their information estimators and optimization procedures. ASIG (Hartmann et al., 2026) amortizes BED into an LLM policy using generative model derived from the policys predictive distributions; its evaluated configuration combines one-step EIG with multi-step task-outcome reward. We instead explicitly optimize the reasoning preceding design selection and specify the training generative model independently of the policy, using fixed contrastive prior and separate semantic likelihood evaluator. This construction enables expected information rewards over the finite hypothesis and outcome spaces, which we accumulate into information-only multi-step returns. Amortized sequential experimental design. Policy-based BED learns adaptive designs across an experiment, shifting optimization to training and accounting for the information available from future observations (Foster et al., 2021; Blau et al., 2022; Ivanova et al., 2021). This includes both tractable-likelihood and implicit-simulator settings. Semi-amortized approaches additionally refine pretrained design policy using observations from the ongoing experiment (Hedman et al., 2025). We build on the fully amortized formulation, studying how its policy, generative model, and information objective should be instantiated for reasoning LLMs with natural-language actions. Task-oriented exploration and interaction learning. Complementary approaches train curious or collaborative agents using task-oriented rewards, including objectives that assess the consequences of an action through future interactions (Tajwar et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025). Successful interaction traces also provide supervision for learning clarifying questions (Andukuri et al., 2024). These works show that strategic information gathering can be learned without an explicit BED objective, and that learned behavior can transfer across tasks (Tajwar et al., 2025). Our focus is instead on the construction of information-only training returns and their effect on acquisition, reasoning, and transfer. External models for information gathering. Prior work combines language models with parametric Bayesian preference models or learned predictive models for adaptive elicitation (Handa et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). Retriever-coupled approaches similarly derive question-training signals from an external candidate distribution or retrieval objective (Chi et al., 2024). These provide precedents for separating language generation from information-value estimation. Our construction uses specified finite hypothesis space and separate semantic likelihood evaluator during training, while deployment requires neither that hypothesis space nor retrieval-based question selection. Estimating information value. Variational and contrastive objectives make Bayesian design optimization tractable (Foster et al., 2019; 2020), while nested Monte Carlo analysis characterizes challenges in estimating information utilities (Rainforth et al., 2018); Rainforth et al. (2024) survey these approaches.

sections.title: D ADDITIONAL DISCUSSION OF THE DESIGN POLICY
sections.content: The previous section identified two challenges that motivate amortizing BED: inhibitive inference time and myopic design selection. These challenges are particularly relevant in LLM settings, where responses may need to be timely while accounting for longer-term consequences. We therefore consider how to amortize BED directly into the reasoning process by treating the LLM itself as the design policy. This requires us to consider the LLM setting. What makes learning LLM design policy unique? Compared to conventional design policies, LLM design policies differ significantly in the design space. Conventional design policies typically map state ht1 directly to design xt from predefined design space ; for instance, Blau et al. (2022) study designs in two-dimensional space. In contrast, when the policy is language model, designs are expressed in an unconstrained natural-language space. Moreover, reasoning LLM policy can generate an intermediate reasoning process that precedes its final design choice. Making this intermediate reasoning an explicit part of the policy output enables an important capability: the policy can be rewarded not only for the final design but also for the reasoning zt that produced it. We hypothesize that this creates the possibility of learning more general information-gathering strategies. We therefore parameterize the policy as πϕ(zt, xt; ht1) = πϕ(zt; ht1) πϕ(xt; ht1, zt), (9) where zt denotes the models reasoning trace2. In other words, the model first reasons over the interaction history and then selects design conditioned on both the history and this reasoning. Employing this LLM design policy requires addressing two design questions (DQs): DQ1: How should the joint distribution p(y, θ; x) be constructed? (Sec. D.1) Computing the (total) EIG requires specifying the joint distribution over hypotheses and experimental outcomes p(y, θ; x). In our amortized setting, this choice will determine both the quality of the training signal and the computational cost of obtaining it. DQ2: How can we provide non-myopic objective? (Sec. D.2) non-myopic objective requires assigning value to current design according to information that may only be acquired in future experiments. This is classic credit-assignment problem in RL, often addressed by estimating future returns through learned value functions. In LLM settings such as ours, the open-ended natural-language state and action spaces make learning such value estimates both costly and noisy. D.1 CONSTRUCTING THE EXPERIMENTAL GENERATIVE MODEL We require generative model of the experiment to define the distribution under which information gain is evaluated. Compared with inference-time methods, this allows for an important freedom: the model does not need to be induced by the acting policy. The experimental generative model can therefore be specified independently as part of the training environment. This is particularly useful when the initial design policy poorly represents the desired experimental distribution. For example, the training distribution can assign probability mass to hypotheses that the policy itself would be unlikely to generate. Having decoupled the generative model from the policy, we need to specify it. The experimental generative model admits two factorizations, p(θ, x) = p(θ) p(y θ, x) = p(y x) p(θ y, x). (10) If the components are estimated separately rather than derived from common joint, the two constructions are not necessarily equivalent. The appropriate factorization therefore depends on which quantities can be obtained reliably and efficiently, as discussed in great detail in BED LLM (Choudhury et al., 2025). We adopt the factorization p(θ)p(y θ, x). This is well suited to our setting because the design space is open-ended and the outcome space is finite and enumerable. For any proposed design and 2Following Choudhury et al. (2025), we use ; to denote general dependence and reserve for probabilistic conditioning under specified joint distribution. This distinction is important for LLM-induced distributions, where including variable in the prompt will influence the model output, but does not in general correspond to conditioning common underlying joint distribution between variables. 29 Preprint. hypothesis θ, the training environment can therefore evaluate the complete distribution over possible outcomes p(y θ, x). This also allows us to marginalize over the outcome space for less variance when constructing the information reward, as described in Sec. D.2. The prior p(θ). Following Blau et al. (2022), we represent the hypothesis distribution using finite contrastive set {θℓ}L ℓ=0 drawn from the desired prior p(θ). The contrastive set can be specified once before policy optimization. This makes the hypothesis distribution itself controllable component of the training environment. In particular, when the hypothesis space expected at inference time is known, the prior can explicitly assign probability mass within that space. In our experiments, we use uniform prior over this contrastive set. We specifically consider hypotheses from Choudhury et al. (2025), although in general the set can be constructed from any available prior knowledge or generative model. The likelihood p(y θ, x). For open-ended natural-language designs, the space of possible designs cannot generally be enumerated in advance, making it impractical to specify likelihood beforehand. We therefore use separate LLM as semantic likelihood evaluator poracle(y; θ, x) which can be queried during training. As in Choudhury et al. (2025), we retain the full stochastic likelihood to account for cases where the outcome is not deterministic even when θ is known. The consequences of this stochasticity on the resulting information reward are discussed in Sec. D.2. D.2 NON-MYOPIC INFORMATION RETURNS With the generative model specified in Sec. D.1, we now have the contrastive hypotheses and corresponding likelihoods poracle(y; θ, x) required to evaluate the sequential contrastive reward in Eq. 4. In Blau et al. (2022), this reward is evaluated for realized outcome. In our setting, the outcome space is enumerable, and the likelihood evaluator provides the full distribution over for each contrastive hypothesis. We can therefore average the one-step reward over possible outcomes, resulting in Rao-Blackwellized information reward which by construction has reduced variance. To construct non-myopic objective, Blau et al. (2022) use an actor-critic method to estimate the expected cumulative future information reward associated with each design. For language policies, critic must estimate future information value over large and highly structured natural-language state-action space. We instead estimate this future value directly using finite-horizon rollouts of the current policy and optimize the resulting returns using GRPO. Starting from history ht1, the policy generates reasoning trace and design, (zt, xt) πϕ( ht1), after which the policy and environment are rolled forward for up to 1 additional experiments. We assign the initial decision the return Rt,K,γ = K1 (cid:88) k=0 γkrt+k. (11) determines the number of experimental steps included in the return and γ controls the relative weight placed on information obtained further into the future. For each training history, GRPO samples group of initial decisions. Each decision is evaluated by its corresponding K-step information return, and the relative returns within the group are used to update the policy. D.3 FIXED CONTRASTIVE SETS AS FINITE BAYESIAN MODELS Standard sPCE constructs finite contrastive approximation by sampling hypotheses from the prior for each trajectory. In our setting, we instead fix single contrastive set throughout training, and define finite prior over this set.
